editorial_note: A curated learning map, not an exhaustive literature review. Questions and takeaways are editorial prompts; citations support the stated claims, not every possible interpretation.

kinds.observation: A measured result, interpreted with stated methods.
kinds.model: An explanatory framework with assumptions and a scope.
kinds.mechanism: A process that accounts for how something happens.
kinds.principle: A constraint with explicit conditions of application.
kinds.open-question: An unresolved question, not evidence for a preferred answer.

nodes.label: Entangled particles violate a Bell inequality
nodes.claim: A 2015 experiment measured spin correlations incompatible with a Bell inequality, closing the major detection and locality loopholes.
nodes.scope: Entangled electron spins separated by 1.3 km.
nodes.limits: The inference still relies on assumptions, including independence of measurement settings.
nodes.question: Which assumption would a competing explanation have to give up?

nodes.label: Quantum states predict outcome probabilities
nodes.claim: Quantum theory predicts correlations using states, measurement operators and a probability rule; entangled states need not factor into independent parts.
nodes.scope: Specified preparations and measurements.
nodes.limits: Successful probabilities do not uniquely select an interpretation of the quantum state.
nodes.question: What does a successful prediction tell us about what exists?

sources.supports: Agreement of measured correlations with quantum predictions.

assumptions: The preparation and measurement are adequately modelled.

nodes.label: The environment suppresses observable interference
nodes.claim: Interactions entangle a system with its environment, reducing interference between alternatives in its reduced description.
nodes.scope: A specified system–environment split.
nodes.limits: Decoherence alone does not select one unique outcome in every interpretation.
nodes.question: Is losing access to interference the same thing as selecting an outcome?

nodes.label: What accounts for a definite measurement outcome?
nodes.claim: Interpretations disagree about how definite records relate to quantum dynamics.
nodes.scope: Foundations of quantum measurement.
nodes.limits: This is not evidence that a conscious mind causes collapse.
nodes.question: What observation could distinguish interpretations that currently predict the same results?

sources.supports: The measurement problem and competing interpretations.

nodes.label: Higher clocks tick at a different rate
nodes.claim: NIST measured a clock-rate difference with optical clocks at heights differing by 33 centimetres, consistent with gravitational time dilation.
nodes.scope: Weak gravity near Earth.
nodes.limits: This test probes a limited regime, not every prediction of relativity.
nodes.question: What must a theory of time explain if two good clocks disagree?

nodes.label: Gravity is described by spacetime geometry
nodes.claim: General relativity relates spacetime curvature to matter and energy and predicts clock shifts and gravitational waves.
nodes.scope: A classical description of gravitation.
nodes.limits: The tests here do not establish a quantum description of gravity.
nodes.question: How far can a theory be trusted beyond the conditions tested?
assumptions: Spacetime can be treated as a smooth classical geometry.

nodes.label: Two detectors measured a merging-black-hole signal
nodes.claim: GW150914 was recorded in 2015; its waveform matched a binary black hole merger predicted by general relativity.
nodes.scope: A transient strain signal at the two LIGO detectors.
nodes.limits: The interpretation uses waveform models and detector-noise analysis.
nodes.question: Why is agreement between independent detectors valuable?

sources.supports: Detection and physical interpretation of GW150914.

nodes.label: Hot gas and inferred mass separate in a cluster collision
nodes.claim: In the Bullet Cluster, X-ray-emitting gas is displaced from the main mass peaks inferred through gravitational lensing.
nodes.scope: A merging galaxy-cluster system.
nodes.limits: Lensing reconstructs mass using a gravitational model; it does not photograph a dark particle.
nodes.question: How can two measurements of the same object test different explanations?

nodes.label: Additional weakly collisional matter explains the offset
nodes.claim: A dark-matter component can pass through the collision while gas slows down, accounting for the separation.
nodes.scope: Cluster dynamics interpreted with standard gravity.
nodes.limits: Evidence for additional gravitating matter does not identify its microscopic nature.
nodes.question: What would count as identifying the substance, beyond inferring its gravity?
assumptions: The gravitational model and mass reconstruction are adequate.

nodes.label: What is the inferred dark component?
nodes.claim: The cluster evidence does not specify a particle species or microscopic theory.
nodes.scope: The inference made by this cluster study.
nodes.limits: An alternative must also explain the measured lensing and gas distribution.
nodes.question: What additional measurement would separate candidate explanations?

sources.supports: The observation establishes no particle identity.

nodes.label: Resetting a physical bit produces measurable heat
nodes.claim: A colloidal-particle experiment tested the heat cost of erasing one bit and approached the Landauer limit in slow resets.
nodes.scope: A controlled two-state memory in a thermal bath.
nodes.limits: This is not a measurement of the energy used by a modern processor.
nodes.question: Which details make a physical experiment a test of an abstract bit?

sources.supports: Experimental reset protocol and heat measurement.

nodes.label: Erasing an unknown bit has a thermodynamic cost
nodes.claim: Resetting an unbiased bit in an ideal cyclic memory dissipates at least k_B T ln(2) of heat on average in the reversible limit.
nodes.scope: Isothermal reset with a thermal bath at temperature T.
nodes.limits: Not a universal energy charge for every computation; correlations and biased memories change the accounting.
nodes.question: Why does forgetting differ from moving or copying information?

nodes.label: How close can a real memory get to that bound?
nodes.claim: The ideal reset limit leaves engineering questions about speed, reliability and the rest of the device.
nodes.scope: Applying a bit-reset result to useful hardware.
nodes.limits: This map offers no performance forecast for current chips.
nodes.question: What system boundary would make an energy-per-operation comparison honest?

sources.supports: Slow-reset result motivates, rather than resolves, the engineering question.

nodes.label: A bacterial population evolved a new way to use citrate
nodes.claim: One long-term E. coli population evolved aerobic citrate use; replay experiments investigated the role of its earlier history.
nodes.scope: A particular population and laboratory environment.
nodes.limits: One innovation is not a replay of all evolutionary history.
nodes.question: How can frozen ancestors turn a historical claim into an experiment?

nodes.label: Earlier changes can alter what becomes accessible
nodes.claim: Genetic history can affect the probability that a later innovation evolves.
nodes.scope: The citrate-use lineage studied here.
nodes.limits: Contingency does not mean every outcome is equally likely.
nodes.question: What difference would you expect between replaying early and late ancestors?

nodes.label: How repeatable is evolution?
nodes.claim: The degree of repeatability depends on the trait, starting population and environment.
nodes.scope: Generalizing from a specific laboratory result.
nodes.limits: The experiment cannot establish that every major innovation was inevitable or impossible to repeat.
nodes.question: What would you hold constant in a fair replay?

sources.supports: The study provides a bounded example, not a universal answer.

nodes.label: Competing theories faced an agreed experimental test
nodes.claim: A 2025 adversarial collaboration tested preregistered predictions from two consciousness theories and challenged key predictions of both.
nodes.scope: Visual experience studied using several brain-measurement methods.
nodes.limits: This was not a decisive explanation of subjective experience.
nodes.question: Why agree on a prediction before seeing the measurements?

nodes.label: Global neuronal workspace theory
nodes.claim: GNWT connects conscious access with information becoming broadly available across brain systems.
nodes.scope: A theory with experimentally testable neural predictions.
nodes.limits: The tested predictions faced challenges; reportability is not the whole question of experience.
nodes.question: Which result would challenge the proposed mechanism?

sources.supports: The model of global availability and conscious access.
GNWT predictions tested in the study.

assumptions: The selected neural signatures adequately operationalize the theory.

nodes.label: Integrated information theory
nodes.claim: IIT links experience to intrinsic causal structure; the study tested selected neural predictions motivated by the theory.
nodes.scope: An active theoretical proposal.
nodes.limits: The experiment did not directly measure the full intrinsic causal structure of a brain.
nodes.question: How much of a theory is tested when only a proxy is measurable?

sources.supports: The theoretical account of intrinsic causal structure.

assumptions: The selected neural signatures adequately operationalize the theory.

nodes.label: What would distinguish an explanation of experience?
nodes.claim: A useful next test needs predictions that separate competing accounts.
nodes.scope: Comparing scientific theories of consciousness.
nodes.limits: A neural correlation alone does not settle every philosophical question.
nodes.question: What could each theory predict incorrectly?

edges.explanation: Measured correlations agree with quantum predictions.
Quantum interactions describe entanglement with an environment.
Suppression of interference alone does not pick a unique outcome.
The measured clock shift agrees with the gravitational prediction.
The observed waveform matches the merger prediction.
Interpreting lensing as mass requires a theory of gravity.
The gas–mass separation favors an additional weakly collisional component under standard gravity.
A gravitational explanation does not determine a microscopic identity.
Controlled resets approach the theoretical heat bound.
A limiting reset cost is insufficient to specify a practical device.
Replay experiments probe whether earlier changes affect innovation.
A contingent laboratory outcome does not determine repeatability everywhere.
Some preregistered GNWT predictions were not met.
Some preregistered IIT predictions were not met.
These accounts motivate different experimental predictions.
The study leaves further discriminating tests necessary.
The study leaves further discriminating tests necessary.

paths.title: Does measurement require a mind?
paths.subtitle: Quantum physics
paths.intro: Start with an experiment, then separate successful predictions from interpretations.
paths.takeaway: Nothing in this path establishes that consciousness causes quantum collapse.

paths.title: Can two good clocks disagree?
paths.subtitle: Relativity
paths.intro: Test a theory of time on a laboratory bench, then follow it to a black hole merger.
paths.takeaway: Confidence grows through different tests; it remains tied to the regimes actually tested.

paths.title: How do we infer matter we cannot see?
paths.subtitle: Cosmology
paths.intro: Separate the light we record, the mass we infer and the substance we have yet to identify.
paths.takeaway: A strong inference about gravity can coexist with uncertainty about the underlying substance.

paths.title: Does forgetting have a physical cost?
paths.subtitle: Information & heat
paths.intro: Follow an abstract bit into a physical memory and ask where its heat goes.
paths.takeaway: A fundamental limit needs a stated process and system boundary before it becomes useful.

paths.title: Could evolution have turned out differently?
paths.subtitle: Evolution
paths.intro: Use a replayable experiment to investigate a question about history.
paths.takeaway: Known mechanisms can permit several histories. Explaining an outcome is not the same as predicting it.

paths.title: What would test a theory of consciousness?
paths.subtitle: Consciousness
paths.intro: Look for a prediction that competing theories cannot both accommodate.
paths.takeaway: Distinguish a theory, the measurable prediction chosen to test it and the result of that test.
